questions.subject: MICROECONOMICS
questions.topic: Labour demand and the marginal product
questions.learningObjective: explain why the labour demand curve slopes downward
questions.stem: A firm's demand curve for labour slopes downward even though every worker is paid the same money. What underlying production fact makes the curve slope?

options.text: The marginal product of the next worker is smaller than the last one's
Workers of the same skill take different amounts of pride in the job
options.misconception: believes morale differences explain a downward labour demand curve

options.text: The firm replaces its most productive workers with cheaper recruits
options.misconception: believes firms routinely downgrade their existing workforce

options.text: The wage a firm offers falls as more workers apply for the job
options.misconception: believes an application queue pushes offered wages down

questions.explanation: A firm hires a worker as long as the revenue that worker's output adds exceeds the wage. Because the marginal product of labour falls as more workers crowd the same plant, the marginal revenue product falls, so the highest wage the firm is willing to pay declines with each additional worker. The curve therefore slopes downward through the points where the marginal revenue product equals the wage. Nothing about the workers' quality or the wage scale causes it: a firm paying one rate for a grade simply stops hiring at the point where the next worker would add less revenue than that rate costs.
questions.hint: Ask what the next worker adds to revenue compared with what the wage costs.

questions.subject: MICROECONOMICS
questions.topic: A wage above the clearing level
questions.learningObjective: explain the unemployment a wage above equilibrium creates
questions.stem: Suppose a wage floor is set above the level at which a labour market used to clear. What must the market look like at that higher wage?

options.text: Firms want more labour than people offer, so overtime appears
options.misconception: believes a wage floor creates a labour shortage

options.text: More people want to work than firms want, so a queue forms
Firms raise output until the extra workers are absorbed at that wage
options.misconception: believes demand is horizontal at a fixed wage

options.text: The queue disappears, since a higher wage attracts extra vacancies
options.misconception: believes a binding floor improves matching in the market

questions.explanation: At a wage above the clearing level the quantity of labour supplied rises along the supply curve and the quantity demanded falls along the downward-sloping demand curve, so supply exceeds demand. The difference is the number of workers willing to take the job who are not wanted for it, and it appears as a queue of applicants or as involuntary joblessness. Employment is set by the short side of the market, which is demand, so the firms that do hire are the ones whose marginal revenue product clears the higher wage, and the workers who lose out are those whose productivity is lowest.
questions.hint: Trace what a wage above the crossing point does to each side of the market separately.

questions.subject: MICROECONOMICS
questions.topic: The two claimed effects of a minimum wage
questions.learningObjective: state the standard effects of a binding minimum wage
questions.stem: Supporters of a minimum wage make two distinct claims about its effects. Which pair of claims is the standard one?

options.text: The pay of covered workers falls, and employment rises with it
options.misconception: believes a binding floor cuts the wage of those it covers

options.text: The pay of every worker rises, and total output rises to match
options.misconception: believes a floor guarantees a raise to the entire workforce

options.text: The pay of covered workers rises, and employment of the least productive falls
The pay of covered workers rises, and total employment cannot change
options.misconception: believes a fixed wage leaves the number hired unchanged

questions.explanation: A binding minimum wage does exactly two things in the standard competitive model. It raises the wage of everyone it covers who was previously paid below it, which is the effect its supporters want, and it raises the cost of hiring above what the least productive workers add to revenue, so those jobs disappear. Because firms are price takers for the wage, an imposed wage cannot leave employment untouched: the demand curve slopes down, so a higher price on the labour market buys a smaller quantity of it. Where the market was already paying above the floor, the law changes nothing at all.
questions.hint: Ask which way the wage moves and which way the quantity of labour firms want moves.

questions.subject: MICROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: explain the mechanism that sustains an above-market efficiency wage
questions.stem: A firm pays 6 percent above the going rate and finds its output per worker higher than at the going rate. How can paying above the market be self-financing?

options.text: The higher pay lets the firm hire the most skilled workers in the market
options.misconception: believes an efficiency wage is just a sorting device for talent

options.text: The higher pay is required by law, so rivals pay it as well
options.misconception: believes efficiency wages arise from a statutory floor

options.text: Workers accept less pay in exchange for more training and promotion
options.misconception: believes above-market pay needs a compensating benefit

options.text: The higher pay cuts turnover and shirking, so measured output rises to match

questions.explanation: An efficiency wage is one where the firm pays above the market because the extra pay buys more than it costs. Workers on that plant are more likely to stay, because leaving means giving up a wage they cannot match elsewhere, and they are more likely to work rather than slack off, because shirking risks dismissal from a job worth keeping. The resulting fall in turnover and rise in effort show up as more output per worker, and if the extra revenue exceeds the extra wage bill the firm gains, so paying above the market can be self-financing rather than a subsidy it has to be given.
questions.hint: Ask what the higher wage does to the cost of quitting and to the incentive to work hard.

questions.subject: MICROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: state the monopsony condition on the wage paid
questions.stem: An employer is the only buyer of labour in its district and must raise its offer to attract more people. What is the telltale sign that it is paying too little?

options.text: The wage it pays is below what the last worker's output adds to revenue
The wage it pays exceeds what the last worker's output adds to revenue
options.misconception: believes overpaying is the usual sign of monopsony power

options.text: The wage it pays equals what the last worker's output adds to revenue
options.misconception: believes a single buyer can always match added revenue

options.text: The wage it pays is set by the government wage board rather than itself
options.misconception: believes statutory wage setting eliminates monopsony power

questions.explanation: A monopsonist faces an upward-sloping labour supply curve because raising its offer is the only way to get more people to apply, so hiring one more worker means paying not only that worker's wage but the higher wage needed to keep the ones it already has. Its marginal factor cost therefore exceeds the wage it actually pays, and it maximises profit where marginal factor cost meets marginal revenue product, which is a smaller workforce and a lower wage than a competitive market would produce. The diagnostic is exactly the gap: the wage sits below the revenue the marginal worker adds, so the firm is exploiting the workers it does hire.
questions.hint: Ask whether the wage the firm pays covers what the last worker's output is worth to the firm.

questions.subject: MICROECONOMICS
questions.topic: Union wage gain and the jobs it costs
questions.learningObjective: trace a negotiated wage through to employment and the wage bill
questions.stem: A district's firms want 280 minus ten times the weekly wage workers, and 20 plus fifteen times that wage workers offer to work. A union lifts the going wage from 12 to 14 dollars. First find the new employment, then report the weekly wage bill at that employment.

options.text: A wage bill of 1,920 dollars, with 160 workers employed
options.misconception: prices the bill at the old employment rather than the new one

options.text: A wage bill of 1,960 dollars, with 140 workers employed
A wage bill of 2,660 dollars, with 190 workers employed
options.misconception: counts everyone willing to work as the number actually employed

options.text: A wage bill of 1,680 dollars, with 120 workers employed
options.misconception: reads the wrong row of the demand schedule as the new employment

questions.explanation: At 12 dollars the market clears, with 160 workers wanted and 160 willing, but at 14 dollars firms want only 280 minus 140, which is 140 workers, so the negotiated wage has cut employment by 20. The wage bill at that employment is 14 times 140, which is 1,960 dollars a week, against 1,920 dollars before, so the total bill rose even as the headcount fell. Employment is set by the short side of the market, which is demand, and the 190 workers willing at 14 dollars are a queue rather than a payroll. A union that wanted to claim it had raised total earnings would have to point to the 1,960 figure, not to the 12 dollar rate.
questions.hint: Find how many workers firms still want at the new wage, then multiply by that wage.

questions.subject: MICROECONOMICS
questions.topic: Coverage of a collective bargaining agreement
questions.learningObjective: distinguish who a bargaining agreement binds
questions.stem: A three-year agreement between one union and one hospital chain covers the chain's cleaners, porters, and nursing assistants. Which statement about its reach is correct?

options.text: It binds every worker in the same occupation across the whole economy
options.misconception: believes a single signature fixes a national wage by itself

options.text: It binds only the union members, leaving the chain free to cut others' pay
options.misconception: believes an agreement leaves the employer wholly unconstrained

options.text: It binds the chain's covered staff and the chain, and reaches no one outside them
It binds the chain only while the union's membership exceeds one half
options.misconception: believes a legal majority threshold controls the contract

questions.explanation: A collective bargaining agreement is a contract between a bargaining unit and an employer, so it binds exactly the workers named in the unit and that employer, and it has no reach beyond them. Workers at another firm in the same occupation, or at the same firm in a different occupation, are outside the agreement unless they are separately included. The set of workers a union can organise therefore decides how much of a firm's labour bill it can bargain over, which is why organising drives the union's leverage and why non-members can still benefit indirectly when the agreed rate becomes a reference point for other deals.
questions.hint: Ask which two parties signed and which workers the unit explicitly names.

questions.subject: MICROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: describe how a binding arbitration award sets a wage
questions.stem: Where talks break down, the parties may submit the dispute to a single arbitrator whose award both sides must implement. How does that settle a wage?

options.text: The arbitrator sets the wage so it always matches the going market rate
options.misconception: believes arbitration is required to reproduce the market price

options.text: The arbitrator votes for the union's figure and the firm may decline it
options.misconception: believes an award is only binding on the side that lost

options.text: The arbitrator reopens the whole wage structure for the entire industry
options.misconception: believes one award must reset every agreement in the trade

options.text: The arbitrator picks a rate between the union's demand and the firm's offer

questions.explanation: Interest arbitration is a settlement device: the arbitrator chooses a wage inside the bargaining range, bounded below by what the employer offered and above by what the union demanded, and both sides are bound to accept it because each would rather take the middle than risk a worse outcome at a strike or a lockout. That is what makes it useful when the parties prefer a compromise to a costly showdown, and it is distinct from interest arbitration in the legal sense of imposing a third party's preference, which is not how the economic mechanism works. The bound is the reason the outcome has to be acceptable to both, and the result is a decision neither side wanted to make alone.
questions.hint: Ask why each side would accept a figure it did not choose, and what limits the range.

questions.subject: MICROECONOMICS
questions.topic: Interest rate as the rental price of capital
questions.learningObjective: state the interest rate as a price of capital
questions.stem: A business borrows at an interest rate to buy a machine. In what sense is that rate a price, and of what?

options.text: It is the price paid for the use of someone else's money for a period
It is the price of the machine itself expressed as a share of its value
options.misconception: believes the rate is a markup on the capital good's cost

options.text: It is the price a buyer pays for the machine's output each year
options.misconception: believes the rate equals the machine's marginal revenue product

options.text: It is the price of the risk that the machine's output fails to sell
options.misconception: believes the rate prices output uncertainty alone

questions.explanation: An interest rate is a price of capital in exactly the sense that a wage is a price of labour: it is the amount paid per period for the use of a financial claim, and the claim conveys the right to receive a future stream of income. That framing is what makes capital and labour comparable in the firm's decision, because a machine is worth buying only if the value of what it produces exceeds the present value of the payments the firm must make to the people who provided the money. The rate is not a markup on the machine and not its marginal revenue product, though it will normally be pushed up by risk and by expected inflation.
questions.hint: Ask what the borrower receives and over what period, then compare that to a wage.

questions.subject: MICROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: compute the marginal revenue product of a worker
questions.stem: A firm's output is 100 units with 5 workers and 118 units with 6 workers, everything else fixed, and it sells each unit for 5 dollars. What is the marginal revenue product of the sixth worker, in dollars? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: The sixth worker adds 18 units, so the marginal product of labour is 18 units a worker, and the marginal revenue product is 18 units times 5 dollars a unit, which is 90 dollars. Working through revenue instead of output gives the same figure: revenue is 500 dollars with 5 workers and 590 dollars with 6, and the difference is 90 dollars, which is what that one worker contributes at the margin. The units are dollars of added revenue per worker, not dollars an hour and not dollars of total revenue, and a firm should therefore be willing to hire that sixth worker for any wage up to 90 dollars.
questions.hint: Take the change in units, multiply by the selling price, and keep the result in dollars.

questions.subject: MICROECONOMICS
questions.topic: Unemployment from a binding wage floor
questions.learningObjective: measure the employment gap created by a wage floor
questions.stem: In one district, labour demanded is 600 minus three times the weekly wage and labour supplied is 200 plus two times that wage, both in workers. A floor of 90 dollars a week is imposed. How many workers are left without the job they want? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: Before the floor the market cleared at a wage of 80 dollars, where 600 minus 240 and 200 plus 160 both give 360 workers, so 90 dollars is a binding floor rather than a harmless one. At 90 dollars firms want 600 minus 270, which is 330 workers, while 380 workers want the job, since 200 plus 180 is 380. The difference of 380 minus 330 is 50 workers, who are willing to work at the floor but not wanted for it. Employment is limited by demand, so it falls from 360 to 330 even though the wage rises.
questions.hint: Evaluate both schedules at the floor wage and subtract the smaller from the larger.

questions.subject: MICROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: find the employment a monopsonist chooses
questions.stem: A district's sole employer faces a marginal revenue product of 100 minus 0.6 times the number of workers, in dollars, and must offer 20 plus 0.2 times that number to attract them. How many workers does it hire, and how much less than a competitive market pays? Report the number of workers only.
questions.explanation: Because the wage offer rises with headcount, the cost of one more worker exceeds the wage paid, so the marginal factor cost is 20 plus 0.4 times the number of workers. Setting that against the marginal revenue product gives 100 minus 0.6L equal to 20 plus 0.4L, so 1.0L is 80 and the firm hires 80 workers, where both sides equal 52 dollars. A competitive market instead equates the wage offer to the marginal revenue product, which gives 100 workers at a wage of 40 dollars. The firm therefore takes 20 fewer workers and pays 4 dollars less than the market, and at its own choice the wage of 36 dollars sits below the 52 dollars that worker adds.
questions.hint: Build the marginal factor cost from the rising wage offer, then equate it to the marginal revenue product.

questions.subject: MICROECONOMICS
questions.topic: Present value of a future sum
questions.learningObjective: discount a single future payment to today
questions.stem: A rebate of 1,000 dollars arrives exactly four years from now and the annual interest rate is 5%. What is that payment worth today, in dollars? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: Present value is what a future sum is worth today at the market rate, and the rule is to divide the sum by the rate's growth factor over the waiting period. Over four years at 5% a year that factor is 1.05 raised to the fourth, which is 1.2155, so 1,000 dollars is worth 1,000 over 1.2155, which is 822.70 dollars today. The complement route agrees: the one-period discount factor is 1 over 1.05, which is 0.9524, and raising it to the fourth power gives 0.8227, and 0.8227 of 1,000 dollars is 822.70. The back-substitution closes the loop, since 822.70 dollars compounded at 5% for four years returns exactly 1,000, which is why a buyer paying 822.70 and a seller receiving 1,000 can both be satisfied at a 5% rate.
questions.hint: Divide the future sum by the growth factor of the interest rate over the waiting period.

questions.subject: MICROECONOMICS
questions.topic: Present value of a payment stream
questions.learningObjective: discount a stream of equal payments to today
questions.stem: An owner will receive 1,000 dollars at the end of each of the next three years. Using the present value of an annuity formula at a 10% annual rate, what is the stream worth today, in dollars? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: The present value of an annuity is the payment times the annuity factor, which is one minus the discount factor raised to the number of periods, all divided by the rate. Three one-period discount factors of 1 over 1.1, that is 0.9091, give 0.7513, so the factor is one minus 0.7513 over 0.1, which is 2.4869, and 1,000 dollars times that is 2,486.85 dollars today. Adding the three discounted payments separately confirms it: 909.09 plus 826.45 plus 751.31 is 2,486.85. The stream is worth less than its 3,000 dollar face total precisely because the last payment waits three years, and each year's payment is discounted harder than the one before.
questions.hint: Apply the annuity formula, or add up the three discounted payments year by year.

questions.subject: MICROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: apply the net present value rule to a project
questions.stem: A project costs 40,000 dollars today and returns 15,000 dollars at the end of each of the next four years, discounted at 5% a year. What is its net present value, in dollars? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: Net present value is the present value of everything the project brings in, less the present value of everything it costs, and the 40,000 dollar outlay happens today so it enters undiscounted. The four returns discount to 14,285.71 plus 13,605.44 plus 12,957.56 plus 12,340.53, which is 53,189.26 dollars, and subtracting 40,000 leaves 13,189.26. The annuity route gives the same present value directly, since 15,000 times the four-period annuity factor of 3.5459 is again 53,189.26. A positive net present value is the accept signal, because it says the project pays back more than the capital tied up in it once the cost of that capital is charged at the market rate.
questions.hint: Discount each of the four returns to today, add them, and subtract the 40,000 dollar outlay.

questions.subject: MICROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: infer a one-period yield from a bond price
questions.stem: A one-year government note with a 1,000 dollar face value is selling for 950 dollars today and repays 1,000 dollars at maturity. What is its one-year yield, as a percentage? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: The yield is the return relative to what the buyer actually pays, so the 50 dollars of interest is measured against the 950 dollars paid today, and 50 over 950 is 5.263 percent. The other route states the same relation as a discount: 950 over 1,000 is 0.95, and one minus 0.95 is the one-period yield of 5.263 percent. Using the 1,000 dollar face value as the base instead would report 5.0 percent, which is the coupon rate rather than the yield an investor earns at today's price, and it is the base a careless calculation picks up.
questions.hint: Compare what the note pays at maturity with what it costs now, using the purchase price as the base.

questions.subject: MICROECONOMICS
questions.topic: Risk premium on a corporate issue
questions.learningObjective: measure the risk premium as a yield spread
questions.stem: A corporate issue of comparable maturity is yielding 7.25% a year while the government yield over the same term is 4.5%. What risk premium, in percentage points, does the corporate issue carry over the government yield? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: The risk premium is the extra return an investor demands for bearing the risk that the corporate promise is not kept, and it is measured against a comparable default-free yield over the same term. The gap is 7.25 minus 4.5, which is 2.75 percentage points, equivalent to 275 basis points. Comparing the two over the same maturity is what makes the figure meaningful, because a spread between a one-year and a ten-year yield would mix term risk into the risk premium. The premium is a price of risk rather than a return for patience, and it varies with how likely investors think default is.
questions.hint: Subtract the risk-free yield from the risky yield and keep the unit in percentage points.

questions.topic: Reading a wage and employment table
questions.learningObjective: read excess supply of labour off a schedule
questions.stem: A district's record shows labour demanded of 200, 180, 160, 140, and 120 workers and labour supplied of 100, 130, 160, 190, and 220 at weekly wages of 8, 10, 12, 14, and 16 dollars. At a wage of 14 dollars, how many workers want jobs they cannot get?
questions.explanation: At 14 dollars the firms want 140 workers and 190 workers want to work, so the difference is 50 who are willing but not wanted. The table shows why the wage is above the clearing level: the two columns are equal at 12 dollars, where 160 workers are both wanted and willing, and 14 dollars is two dollars above that. The 30 workers per two dollars the supply column adds and the 20 the demand column loses each step are what open the gap. The firms that clear the higher wage are the ones whose marginal revenue product reaches 14 dollars, and the rest of the queue is the unemployment the floor creates.
questions.hint: Subtract the workers wanted at 14 dollars from the workers offering to work at 14 dollars.

questions.topic: Hiring against a marginal revenue product schedule
questions.learningObjective: choose the hire level from a marginal revenue product schedule
questions.stem: A firm's output is 0, 40, 70, 92, 108, and 120 units at 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, and 5 workers, and each unit sells for 8 dollars. At a wage of 150 dollars a worker, how many workers should it hire? Report the number only.

The firm hires while that exceeds the 150 dollar wage, so the first three clear it and the fourth does not, making three workers the right level. Profit confirms it from above rather than repeating the rule: revenue less the wage bill is minus 110 dollars with one worker, minus 140 with two, minus 114 with three, minus 36 with four, and plus 120 with five, so three workers is the peak among the levels the rule allows. The falling sequence of marginal products also shows the diminishing returns behind the downward-sloping demand curve.

questions.subject: MICROECONOMICS
questions.topic: Why a minimum wage cuts employment
questions.learningObjective: refute a claim that a wage floor cannot reduce employment
questions.stem: A councillor argues that a minimum wage cannot reduce employment, because it only raises what a worker is worth and every employer gains from a better worker. Explain what the model of a competitive labour market says instead.

answer.exemplar: The councillor has confused what a worker is worth with what a firm must pay, and the two come apart as soon as the wage is set above the market. What a worker is worth to a firm is the revenue that worker's output adds, which is the marginal revenue product, and it is strictly smaller than the marginal revenue product of the workers already doing the job. A floor above the going rate places the wage above that value for a band of workers, and a firm that is free to hire elsewhere responds by not hiring them at all, so the firm's labour demand curve, which slopes downward, delivers fewer jobs. The exchange is not that the wage rises and employment holds; it is that the wage rises for the workers who keep their jobs and the least productive lose theirs. A second wrong version appeals to fairness as though it settled the employment question, or says employers must therefore be benefiting, when the firms whose marginal revenue product falls below the floor are the ones whose output shrinks.

questions.explanation: A strong answer explains why a firm's willingness to hire falls as the required wage rises, and identifies the band of workers whose productivity is now below the floor. The tempting wrong version says a higher wage can only attract more labour supply and never less demand, which mistakes a movement along the supply curve for the whole market. A second wrong version claims firms are forced to hire at the floor because workers are now worth more, which reverses the direction of the marginal revenue product comparison.
questions.hint: Ask what a worker's output is worth to the firm compared with the wage the firm must now pay.

questions.subject: MICROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: state the present value rule for accepting a project
questions.stem: A firm can fund one project or another from the same pool of money at today's market rate. Which comparison settles which one to take?

options.text: Whether the project's total profit over its life is the larger figure
options.misconception: believes undiscounted totals decide between two investments

options.text: Whether the returns discounted to today exceed the outlay discounted to today
Whether the project pays back its outlay sooner than the alternative
options.misconception: believes the quickest payback is the most valuable project

options.text: Whether the project's first year return beats the market interest rate
options.misconception: believes the first year alone tells the whole story

questions.explanation: Money received later is worth less than the same money received now, so the only like-for-like comparison puts both projects on today's terms: discount every future return and every future cost back to today and take the difference. If that difference is positive the project returns more than the capital tied up in it at the market rate, and if it is negative it destroys value against simply lending the money out. Both halves must be discounted, which is why a project with a large later cost can be worth taking even when its early cash flows look poor.
questions.hint: Ask what the returns are worth today, and what the outlay costs today.

questions.subject: MICROECONOMICS
questions.topic: Internal rate of return and its weakness
questions.learningObjective: state the weakness of ranking projects by internal rate of return
questions.stem: Two projects are compared and the first shows a higher internal rate of return, so it is chosen. What is wrong with that ranking?

options.text: A rate can only be computed for projects with no later cash inflows
options.misconception: believes the rate requires inflows to arrive in year one

options.text: The rate already includes the project's size, so no extra check is needed
options.misconception: believes a percentage return carries a project's scale with it

options.text: A high rate on a small project can add less value than a lower rate on a large one
Two projects may share a single rate, so ranking by it is impossible
options.misconception: believes every pair of projects must have different rates

questions.explanation: The internal rate of return is a percentage, so it carries no information about how much money the project actually involves. A workshop tool that returns 200% on 5,000 dollars creates far less than a plant that returns 12% on 2 million dollars, and choosing on the rate alone can therefore pass up the larger gain. The discount rate comparison has the same blind spot, and the underlying present value difference does not, because it is measured in dollars. A second problem is cash flows that change sign more than once, which can make the rate ambiguous or impossible to define.
questions.hint: Ask how many dollars each project actually involves, not what percentage it returns.

questions.subject: MICROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: state why the payback rule can mislead
questions.stem: A manager screens new projects by how quickly they recover the original outlay, and rejects a long-running one. What does that rule leave out?

options.text: The size of the original outlay that has to be recovered
options.misconception: believes a rule about speed needs no mention of scale

options.text: The interest the firm pays on the money while it is tied up
options.misconception: believes a payback screen already charges a financing cost

options.text: The number of years before the project turns profitable at all
options.misconception: believes the payback date marks the profit-making point

options.text: The value of everything the project earns after the payback date

questions.explanation: The payback rule asks only how long the original outlay is tied up and then stops counting, so it throws away every return that arrives after that date, however large. It also does not discount: a project that returns 30 dollars in year one and 30 in year three is credited the same as one returning 30 in year one and 30 in year two, even though the second is worth more today. The rule is a rough liquidity screen and nothing more, which is why a project with a long wait and large late payoffs is often the best investment available and is routinely rejected by it.

Because beta is built from excess movements rather than levels, the same figure comes from the second observation alone, since the share's 11 point rise over the market's 8 point rise is exactly that ratio. A beta above one means the share amplifies the market, so it should have been expected to fall in a bad year and to fall less than the market's gain would suggest; at a 14% market return the relation predicts 4 plus 1.375 times 12, which is 20.5%.

questions.explanation: Only the part of a share's variance that comes from the market is diversifiable away, and that part is the beta squared times the market's variance, which is 0.64 times 0.02, or 0.0128. The remaining 0.04 minus 0.0128, which is 0.0272, is variance peculiar to the firm, and 0.0272 over 0.04 is 68 percent. The share of the other kind is therefore 32 percent, and the two shares sum to 100 percent as they must. This is the arithmetic behind the diversification argument: holding a single share leaves the holder exposed to both components, while a large portfolio washes out most of the idiosyncratic piece and leaves the systematic one, which no amount of spreading can remove.

questions.topic: Why the internal rate of return is not enough
questions.learningObjective: explain why a higher rate of return need not mean a better project
questions.stem: A committee adopts the rule that the project with the highest internal rate of return gets the funding. Explain, with figures if you like, why that rule can pick the worse of two projects.

answer.exemplar: The rule ranks projects by a percentage and a percentage says nothing about the size of the stake, so a spectacular rate on a trivial amount of capital can be beaten by a modest rate on a large one. Take a 5,000 dollar piece of equipment that returns 10,000 in a year, which is a 100% rate and creates 5,000 dollars of value, and a 2 million dollar plant that returns 240,000 a year forever at a 12% rate against a 10% cost of funds, which creates hundreds of thousands. Sorting by rate puts the small project first, yet the plant is where the money belongs, and the present value difference settles it in the plant's favour while the rate comparison cannot even see the disagreement. A second defect compounds this: a project whose cash flows change sign more than once can have no single rate at all, or several, so the rule does not even return an answer. What the rate is genuinely good for is comparing projects of similar size and similar timing, where the two orderings agree.

questions.explanation: A strong answer shows a case where the higher rate creates less value, and explains that the present value difference is measured in dollars rather than percentages. The tempting wrong version says the rule errs only by ignoring risk, when the deeper problem is that the rate is scale free while investment is not. A second wrong version defends the rule by pointing out that it never needs discounting separately, which confuses it with the present value rule it is meant to approximate.
questions.hint: Ask how many dollars each project involves, and compare what each one adds rather than what it returns as a percentage.

questions.stem: One-year government securities yield 3%, the stock market's expected excess return over that rate is 6%, and a share's beta is 1.75. What return do investors require on that share, as a percentage? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: The required return is the risk-free rate plus the share's beta times the market's excess return, so it is 3 plus 1.75 times 6, which is 3 plus 10.5, or 13.5 percent. The alternative route starts from the market's own expected total return, which is 3 plus 6, or 9 percent, and adds 1.75 times the 6 point excess to reach 13.5 again. A beta of 1.75 is what does the work here: the share swings harder than the market, so the investor demands 10.5 points above the safe rate rather than the market's 6, which is why the required return is far above the market's own expected return.
questions.hint: Add the risk-free rate to the share's beta times the market's excess return.

questions.subject: MICROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: compute an insurer's expected claim across a pool
questions.stem: An insurer's book is 60% careful drivers with a 5% chance each of a 400 dollar claim, and 40% risky drivers with a 30% chance of the same 400 dollar claim. What is the expected claim per driver across the whole book, in dollars? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: A careful driver's expected claim is 0.05 times 400, which is 20 dollars, and a risky driver's is 0.30 times 400, which is 120 dollars, so weighting those by the shares of the book gives 0.6 times 20 plus 0.4 times 120, which is 12 plus 48, or 60 dollars. The other route works from the average probability of loss, which is 0.6 times 0.05 plus 0.4 times 0.30, or 0.15, and 0.15 times the 400 dollar claim is 60 dollars. That pooled figure is the reason an insurer cannot offer the same all-inclusive policy to everyone, since 60 dollars of expected claim against a careful driver's willingness to pay is a very different proposition from the 120 dollars a risky driver will cost.
questions.hint: Find each type's expected claim, then weight the two by their shares of the book.

questions.subject: MICROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: compute a portfolio's expected return from its weights
questions.stem: A fund puts 60% of its money in a share with an expected return of 15% and the remaining 40% in a share with an expected return of 6%. What is the fund's expected return, as a percentage? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: The portfolio's expected return is the weighted sum of the components, so it is 0.6 times 15 plus 0.4 times 6, which is 9 plus 2.4, or 11.4 percent. The same figure follows from dollar weights: 15 percent of 60 plus 6 percent of 40, which is 9 plus 2.4, and 11.4 percent. The result must lie between 6 and 15 because a combination of the two cannot be worse than all of one or better than all of the other, and 11.4 sits between them. Diversification changes risk rather than this arithmetic: the expected return is fixed by the weights, while the variance is not, which is the point the next questions turn on.
questions.hint: Multiply each expected return by its share of the fund and add the two results.

questions.subject: MICROECONOMICS
questions.topic: What a screening device is worth
questions.learningObjective: value a screening device by the sorting it produces
questions.stem: A workshop pays 30 dollars an hour. A worker who concentrates produces 42 dollars of value an hour and one who day-dreams produces 24 dollars, and a 6 dollar test identifies which is which perfectly. What is the firm's profit per hour when it uses the test, in dollars? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: With the test the firm hires the diligent worker, whose 42 dollars of value less the 30 dollar wage leaves 12 dollars, and paying 6 dollars for the test brings that down to 6 dollars an hour. Without the test it cannot tell the two apart, so the value of a randomly chosen worker is the average of 42 and 24, which is 33 dollars, and 33 less 30 is 3 dollars an hour. Sorting is therefore worth 3 dollars an hour to the firm while costing 6, and the difference of exactly 3 between the two figures is what makes the test worth buying: it is profitable whenever it costs less than the gap it closes, here 6 against 12 of mis-sorting avoided.
questions.hint: Take the value the test lets the firm capture, less the wage and less the test's own cost.

questions.subject: MICROECONOMICS
questions.topic: Idiosyncratic variance in a large portfolio
questions.learningObjective: show how a portfolio's firm-specific variance shrinks
questions.stem: Each of 20 shares in a portfolio has an idiosyncratic return variance of 0.04, those firm-specific parts move independently of one another, and the money is split equally. What is the portfolio's idiosyncratic variance, in decimal form? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: Each share carries a weight of one twentieth, so its contribution to portfolio variance is its squared weight times its own variance, which is 0.0025 times 0.04, and twenty such contributions add to 0.002. Because the firm-specific parts are independent there is no cross term between them, so the total is simply twenty times 0.0001, which is 0.002. Dividing by the number of holdings is the whole mechanism, which is why doubling the number of holdings halves the firm-specific variance: a portfolio of one share would show 0.04 and a portfolio of one hundred would show 0.0004, with the market's own variance untouched throughout.
questions.hint: Add each share's squared weight times its own variance, and note that the cross terms vanish.

questions.subject: MICROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: measure the return a benchmark fails to explain
questions.stem: In one year the market portfolio returned 11% while government securities yielded 5%, and a share with a beta of 1.2 returned 4%. How many percentage points of the share's return went beyond what its risk explains? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: The return the share's risk justifies is the risk-free rate plus its beta times the market's excess return, and the market's excess here is 11 minus 5, which is 6 points, so the justified return is 5 plus 1.2 times 6, which is 12.2 percent. The share actually returned 4 percent, so the part the benchmark does not explain is 4 minus 12.2, which is minus 8.2 percentage points. Stripping out the risk-free rate first gives the same figure: the share's excess return was 4 minus 5, which is minus 1, while the justified excess was 1.2 times 6, which is 7.2, and minus 1 minus 7.2 is again minus 8.2.
questions.hint: Predict the return from the risk-free rate and the beta, then subtract it from what actually happened.

questions.subject: MICROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: read an insurer's exposure off a risk table
questions.stem: An insurer's table shows careful drivers at 70% of the book with a 5% chance of a 600 dollar claim, and risky drivers at 30% with a 25% chance of the same claim. What is the expected claim per driver across the whole book, and is that figure higher than the claim a careful driver causes?
questions.explanation: A careful driver's expected claim is 0.05 times 600, which is 30 dollars, and a risky driver's is 0.25 times 600, which is 150 dollars, so the book as a whole costs 0.7 times 30 plus 0.3 times 150, which is 21 plus 45, or 66 dollars a driver. The average probability route agrees: 0.7 times 0.05 plus 0.3 times 0.25 is 0.11, and 0.11 times 600 is 66. The figure is more than twice what a careful driver alone costs, which is precisely the obstacle to charging one price for full cover. An insurer that prices to the 66 dollar average is offering a policy the careful drivers find excellent and the risky drivers cannot refuse, and the losses will come from the group that costs it the most.
questions.hint: Find each type's expected claim, weight the two by their shares of the book, and compare with the careful figure alone.

questions.subject: MICROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: trace the price collapse in a market for lemons
questions.stem: A used car lot is half sound cars worth 1,200 dollars to buyers and half shakier cars worth 400, and buyers cannot tell them apart. What price do the remaining cars eventually fetch once the lot has sorted itself out?
questions.explanation: With the lot half and half, a buyer who cannot sort the cars will pay the average of 1,200 and 400, which is 800 dollars, and at that price a sound car's owner is losing 400 dollars a sale and simply keeps the car. As those owners withdraw, the share of shakier cars climbs towards all of the lot, and a buyer facing an all-shaky lot will pay only 400 dollars. The lot has not gone quiet, but its average quality has collapsed to the worst cars it ever held and every sound car has been driven out of the market, which is why unverifiable quality destroys a market that was previously clearing.
questions.hint: Ask what price a buyer pays when only the least sound cars are left to look at.

questions.subject: MICROECONOMICS
questions.topic: Backing a beta out of a required return
questions.learningObjective: solve the pricing relation for beta
questions.stem: Investors require 11.5% a year on a share, one-year government securities yield 4%, and the stock market's expected return is 12%. Using the capital asset pricing relation, what is the share's beta? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: Rearranging the pricing relation so that the excess return required of the share is divided by the market's excess return gives beta, and the share's excess is 11.5 minus 4, which is 7.5 points, while the market's is 12 minus 4, which is 8 points, so beta is 7.5 over 8, or 0.9375. Substituting it back confirms the figure: 4 plus 0.9375 times 8 is 4 plus 7.5, which is 11.5 percent as required. A beta just under one means the share is very slightly less risky than the market as a whole, which is why its required return sits a little below the market's 12 percent rather than above it.
questions.hint: Divide the share's required return less the risk-free rate by the market's return less the same rate.

questions.subject: MICROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: refute a claim that market risk makes diversification pointless
questions.stem: A columnist argues that because a diversified holder still carries the market's risk, spreading money across shares achieves nothing and any single stock will do. Explain what the risk-diversification logic says about that claim.

answer.exemplar: The columnist concedes the premise and then draws the wrong conclusion from it, because the question is not whether a diversified portfolio is risk free but how much risk it carries. A share's return has two parts, one driven by the market and one driven by its own firm, and the second part is close to independent across firms, so spreading money averages it away while leaving the first part untouched. A holder of one share carries that firm's entire idiosyncratic variance on top of the market's, and if that firm is unlucky the whole holding suffers; a holder of fifty shares has almost none of it left. Since investors are risk averse they would rather hold the same expected return with less total risk, so the diversified portfolio is strictly preferred, and it is preferred even though the market risk in it cannot be diversified away. The market's risk sets the floor on what any holder must bear, not a reason to prefer concentrating the avoidable part.

questions.explanation: A strong answer separates the diversifiable and non-diversifiable parts of risk and shows that holding one asset adds the avoidable part on top of the unavoidable one. The tempting wrong version says a diversified portfolio is safe, which overstates the case and would make the columnist's point about concentration look right. A second wrong version says diversification raises the expected return, when it changes only the risk, leaving the weighted average return untouched.
questions.hint: Ask how a single share's risk compares with the market's alone, and whether the extra part is avoidable.

questions.subject: MICROECONOMICS
questions.topic: Why a signal must be costly
questions.learningObjective: state the requirement for a credible signal
questions.stem: An employer offers a free training badge to any worker who asks for one, and finds that almost everyone takes it. Explain why the badge sorts nobody, and what a credible signal would need instead.

answer.exemplar: A signal only sorts people if it is more expensive for the people it is meant to exclude than for the people it is meant to identify, and a free badge on request has no such asymmetry. Everyone can obtain it, so possession carries no information: the employer cannot tell a diligent applicant from a careless one, and the badge's only effect is to add a queue. What a credible signal needs is a cost the excluded type finds harder or dearer to bear, so a qualification that requires real study separates those who can do the work from those who cannot, a deposit that only a confident applicant risks separates the sure from the desperate, and a warranty that only a seller with nothing to hide will offer separates the honest from the rest. The badge could be made to work that way, but only by attaching a cost, which is why hiring examinations, training bonds, and second-hand warranties all price the sorting they perform. A free requestable badge is not a weak signal; it is not a signal at all.

questions.explanation: A strong answer states the cost asymmetry a signal needs and shows that a free on-request badge has none, then gives examples of costly alternatives. The tempting wrong version says the badge is a signal that simply carries no weight because few workers bother to take it, which reverses the problem: the issue is that everyone can. A second wrong version proposes collecting a small fee, without noticing that a small fee does not separate anyone either.
questions.hint: Ask who would find the signal hardest to obtain, and whether anyone who wanted it could get it.

questions.learningObjective: compare a careful driver's claim with the pool premium
questions.stem: An insurer's book is 70% careful drivers with a 5% chance of a 600 dollar claim and 30% risky drivers with a 25% chance of the same, and it charges every driver a flat 80 dollar premium with full cover. First find a careful driver's expected claim, then report how far that falls short of the premium.

options.text: A 30 dollar expected claim, falling 20 dollars short of the premium
options.misconception: adds the risky drivers' expected claim into the careful figure by mistake

options.text: A 66 dollar expected claim, falling 14 dollars short of the premium
options.misconception: reports the pool's average claim instead of a careful driver's own

options.text: A 30 dollar expected claim, falling 50 dollars short of the premium
A 150 dollar expected claim, falling 70 dollars short of the premium

questions.explanation: A careful driver costs the insurer 0.05 times 600, which is 30 dollars in expectation, so against a flat 80 dollar premium the insurer is 50 dollars worse off for every careful driver it covers at full terms. Charging the same premium to everyone is what cannot continue, which is why cover is either priced by type or made conditional on behaviour the contract can observe.

options.text: 800 dollars, after an initial price of 800 dollars

options.misconception: averages the two valuations again after the sound cars have gone

options.text: 400 dollars, after an initial price of 1,200 dollars

options.text: 400 dollars, after an initial price of 800 dollars

questions.explanation: A buyer facing an unknown half-and-half lot will pay the average of the two valuations, which is 800 dollars, and that is the only price at which the lot initially clears. At 800 dollars a sound car's owner is being offered 400 dollars less than the car is worth, so those owners withdraw and the lot becomes all shakier cars, which are worth 400 dollars. Buyers then price what is actually left, so the price falls to 400. The market does not close, but the average quality collapses and the good cars are driven out entirely, which is the sense in which one-sided information can destroy a market that was working.
